title: The constant cannot simply be dropped
question: Why does the zero-radiation boundary condition matter?
recap: Inverting Wien’s law and integrating gives the entropy density plus a frequency-dependent constant. Requiring zero entropy density at zero radiation fixes that constant; it does not cancel automatically.
premises: The narrow spectral region obeys the Wien approximation.
At zero radiation density, radiation entropy density vanishes.
limitations: A positive inferred temperature alone is not a guarantee that the Wien approximation is accurate.
The spectral constants are not initially interpreted as particle energies.

overview.text: Inverting Wien’s law and integrating gives the entropy density plus a frequency-dependent constant. Requiring zero entropy density at zero radiation fixes that constant; it does not cancel automatically.

full.spoken: Wien spectral energy density is A times frequency cubed times the exponential of minus B frequency over temperature.

full.spoken: Inverse temperature is minus one over B frequency times the natural logarithm of density over A frequency cubed.
The integrated entropy density is minus density over B frequency times the bracketed logarithm minus one, plus a frequency-dependent constant.

steps.text: Letters: the paper writes Wien's law as \(\rho=\alpha\nu^3e^{-\beta\nu/T}\), with the α and β of §2 (A and B here), and writes lg for the natural logarithm (ln here). The paper notes that observations show this law is not exactly valid, but that for large values of ν/T it was confirmed very completely by experiment. It bases its calculation on the law and keeps in mind that the results hold only within certain limits.

items: Now the boundary condition. As \(\rho_\nu\) falls toward zero, \(\rho\ln\rho\) also falls toward zero, because the logarithm grows more slowly than ρ shrinks, and so does ρ itself. What remains in the limit is C(ν).
